translations.text: By Saint Basil, Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia.

Praise of the Forty Martyrs. O commemoration of the martyrs! How can those who love the martyrs ever have their fill? For honor shown to good fellow servants is plainly also a sign of love for their common Master.
For those who praise valiant men at the appointed times will not refrain from imitating them.

Therefore, sincerely call blessed the martyrdom of the one who suffered, so that you may become a martyr in your will. And without persecution, without fire, without being flayed, you will come forth counted worthy of those same torments.
Our task is to marvel not at one martyr, nor at two, nor at ten: the number of these blessed men is forty.
They had, as it were, one soul in separate bodies, and with one purpose and unity of faith they displayed the same endurance in the face of cruel suffering and the same steadfastness for the truth.

All were equal to one another: equal in will and equal in sufferings. Therefore they were also deemed worthy of an equally honoured crown of glory. What words, then, could ever praise them as they deserve? Not even forty tongues would be enough to sing the virtue of such men.
Even if there were only one to admire, he would be enough to surpass our powers, let alone so great a multitude. [?]
[?], an invincible army, likewise undefeated in battle.
Rather, then, bringing their memory into our midst for the common benefit, let us use their example to build up those present, first setting before everyone
a sketch, as it were, of these men's courage and their valor in battle. For often writers
and painters portray such deeds, the former adorning them with words, the latter drawing them on panels; and both have stirred many to courage.
For what speech shows through narration and hearing, writings show silently through imitation.
In the same way let us remind those present of the virtue of these men, so that, having set their deeds before their eyes, we may be moved to imitate the most valiant.
and draw closer to them through imitation. For the praise of martyrs is the encouragement of those gathered

in virtue. For accounts of the saints do not consent to be governed by the rules of praise, since those who deliver praises take the starting points of their praise from the circumstances of this world.
But for those to whom the world has been crucified, how can anything in it add to their glory? For the saints did not have a single homeland: one came from one

region, another from another. What then? Shall we call them citizens of no city, or citizens of the whole inhabited world? For just as, when people gather to make an offering, what each brings becomes common to all who bring offerings,
so too with these blessed men: each one's homeland belongs to them all, and all, coming from everywhere, share their homelands with one another.
But why do we seek a city for those standing upon [?], passing over their present city, which is spiritual? The martyrs' city is the city of God, whose architect and builder is God:
the Jerusalem above, which is free, the mother of Paul and of those like him.
By human birth, one came from one place and another from another; but their spiritual birth is one for all.
For God is their common father, and they are all brothers: not from one and the same birth, but from spiritual adoption, joined in a union that they themselves formed through love.
A choir ready-made, a great addition to those who glorify the Lord from of old. They were not gathered one by one but changed over suddenly. What was the manner of that change?
These men, in bodily stature, youthful maturity, and strength, were equal to all their companions. All were enrolled in [?] as the better men, also because of their skill in warfare.
and their courage of soul, they received great honors from the emperor,

They were renowned among all for their valour. When there had already been proclaimed, when there had already been proclaimed, that godless and impious decree that Christ must not be named, or else one must suffer dangers, every kind of torture was threatened, and much bestial fury was stirred up by the unrighteous against the faithful.

Plots and evil schemes were woven against them, and various kinds of torture were devised, and the torturers were unrelenting. The fire was ready, the sword sharpened, the cross set up; the pit, the wheel, the scourges.
And some fled, while others gave in; some wavered, and others, threatened only with the trial, were terrified.
Others came close to the cruel torments and gave way.

Still others entered the contest but could not endure the pain to the end, and renounced the faith in the middle of their suffering. Like those labouring in the deep sea, they lost the cargo of endurance they had.
Then these invincible and valiant soldiers of Christ came forward into the midst, as the governor was displaying the emperor's letters
and demanding obedience from everyone. With a free voice, boldly and manfully, and not at all frightened by the threats, they came forward into the midst and declared themselves Christians.

Oh, blessed tongues, all those that uttered that holy cry! The air received it and was sanctified; the angels heard it and clapped their hands; the devil and his demons were wounded; and the Lord wrote their names in heaven.
Each of them, stepping out into the middle, said: "I am a Christian." And just as those who go into battle call out their names together,
and so take their places on the field of battle, so too did these men. Then they cast aside the names they had been given at birth, [and took their name] from the Savior common to all.
each named himself.
And they all did this one after another, joining themselves together.
So all of them had one name. No longer was it this one or that one; all were called Christians.
What then did that ruler do? For he was cruel and changeable. At one moment he soothed them with flattery; at another he wanted to turn them by threats.
First he tried to win them over with flattery, attempting to loosen them from their firm stand in the good faith. He said: "Do not throw away your youth, and do not exchange [?] for an untimely [?]
By death. Of this sweet life.
“It is not fitting for men accustomed to victory in battle to die a criminal’s death.” Besides this, he promised gifts, and further, “If you receive honors and high offices from the emperor [?].”
With countless schemes he tried to entice them. But when they did not weaken under that temptation, he turned to another kind of scheme.
He assailed them with wounds, deaths, and immeasurable tortures. Such were the words he spoke.

But the martyr [?] said, “Why do you entice us, you enemy of God, to turn away from the living God and serve destructive demons, setting your good things before us? What can you give that is so great?
Whatever you strive to take away. I hate such a gift, which brings loss. I do not accept honor that is the mother of dishonor.
Do you give gifts that will be left behind? Glory that will be left behind? Do you make us known to the emperor? But you lead us away from the true King.
Why do you offer small things and give us so little of this world? We care nothing for the whole world. To us, the things that can be seen do not equal the hope we long for.
"Do you see this sky, how good and how great it is to look at? And the earth, how great it is, and all the wonderful things on it?"
"Nothing of all that is equal to the blessedness [?]
of the righteous. For these things pass away, but ours endure.
I desire one gift: the crown of righteousness. I wish to see one glory: the kingdom of heaven.
I love the heavenly honor greatly. I fear the torments of Gehenna. I am terrified of that fire. But I do not fear the fire you threaten me with, for it is my fellow-servant; it knows how to revere
those who disregard idols. Your blows are no more to me than children's arrows.
For it is the body that you strike. If it endures courageously, it receives a more glorious crown; but if it dies suddenly,
it will depart, having escaped cruel judges. Having been entrusted with bodily service, do you attempt to rule over souls as well? Do you set yourselves above our God?
Having received the utmost insult from us, you are indignant and threaten us with these terrible tortures, charging us with the sin of
…piety. But the things you threaten are not fearful, not terrible, not frightening.
For the love of God, see, we are ready to be bound to the wheel, to be bound and burned, and to accept every form of torment. When that haughty and fierce man heard this,
Unable to bear the men’s boldness, and boiling over with rage, he considered what scheme he might devise to prolong their [?].
death prolonged. He devised a plan. See how cruel it was.

For he considered the nature of that country, how bitterly cold it was there, and that the season was winter. He chose the night, when the cold becomes especially severe; moreover, a north wind was blowing that night.
he ordered them all to be stripped naked and to freeze to death in the open in the middle of the city.
But all of you who have experienced winter know how severe this kind of torture is.
For no one can explain it except those who have experienced it.
When the body is exposed to the cold, it first turns entirely blue as the blood congeals; then it becomes agitated and boils.
The teeth chatter, the sinews contract, and the whole body shakes involuntarily. Sudden, fierce, indescribable pain reaches the very limbs, making sensation painful for those who are freezing.
Then the extremities of the body fall off, as though burned by blazing fire. For the warmth is driven away from the ends of the body
and flees into its depths, leaving dead the parts from which it has withdrawn and bringing pain to those it enters, as death gradually approaches through freezing. Then they were sentenced

to stand out in the open all night, while a fierce north wind blew without ceasing. There was a lake beside which the city had been built, where these saints suffered. It had become like a plain for horses to run across: the frost had transformed it, and it had frozen so hard that people and beasts of burden walked over it. The ever-flowing rivers stopped, frozen solid, and the soft substance of water was transformed into something resembling stone. The fierce north wind blew, driving everything that had life in it toward death. Then, when they heard the command—look here at the men’s invincibility!—each joyfully cast off even his last shirt, and they went toward death by freezing as though going to seize treasure, encouraging themselves and saying:
“Are we merely stripping off our clothes? No, we are putting off the old self, corrupted by deceitful desires.
We praise you, Lord, as we strip sin from ourselves along with this clothing.

Since we clothed ourselves because of the serpent, let us strip ourselves for Christ’s sake. Let us not spare our clothes for the sake of the paradise we lost. What shall I give back to the Lord? Our Lord too was stripped.
What great thing is it for a servant to undergo the same thing as his lord? Indeed, we ourselves stripped the Lord, for [?] dared to do this.
They stripped him and divided his clothes. Let us, then, put away through ourselves the great reproach recorded against us.
The winter is bitter, but paradise is sweet. Freezing is painful, but rest is pleasant.
Let us wait a little, and the embrace of Abraham the patriarch will shelter us. For one night we shall receive all eternity in exchange.
"Let the foot be burned, so that it may dance forever with the angels. Let the hand be cut off, so that it may have the boldness
to be lifted up to the Master. How many of our soldiers have fallen in battle, keeping faith in friendship with a corruptible king!"
But we, for loyalty to the true King—
will I not give up this life? How many have suffered a criminal’s death after being arrested for wrongdoing!
shall we not endure for righteousness? Let us not shrink from death, my companions. Let us not give the devil cause for rejoicing. Let us not spare our flesh [?], since in any case we must die.
let us die so that we may live. Let our bodies be a sacrifice before you, Lord, and let us be accepted

As a living sacrifice acceptable to you, we are wholly consumed by this cold: a good offering, a new burnt offering, sacrificed neither by fire nor by cold [?].” Giving one another these comforting words and encouraging one another, as though keeping watch in battle, they passed the night.
enduring their suffering, rejoicing courageously in what they hoped for, and mocking the adversary.
They all had one prayer: “Forty of us entered this struggle; let forty of us be crowned, Master. Let not a single one be missing from our number.”
“Honorable is the number that you have honored with the forty days of fasting through which the Law entered the world.”
“Through forty days of fasting, Elijah sought the Lord and saw the Lord.”
Such was their prayer. But one of their number grew weak and fled from the harsh conditions, departing—a boundless grief to the saints.
The Lord allowed their prayers to be without end.
For a certain man had been posted to guard the martyrs. He was warming himself in a bath somewhere nearby, watching for what would happen, ready to receive any of the soldiers who fled to him.
But this too had been devised: a bath nearby, offering quick help to anyone who fled.
This too the evildoers cunningly devised: to find a place where the comfort ready at hand would weaken them.
It made the endurance of those who were contending appear all the more glorious, the endurance of the martyrs.
For the enduring person is not the one who lacks necessities, but the one who has abundance and yet endures suffering. And so, when
They contended, and he watched.
He saw a marvelous vision of what was happening: certain powers coming down from heaven, as if from an emperor,

handing out great gifts to the soldiers. They gave gifts to all of them, but left just one without honor, saying he was unworthy of the heavenly honors. He at once could not bear the pain and fled over to the enemy.
It was a grievous sight for the righteous: the soldier a deserter, the brave man a captive, the sheep of Christ prey for wild beasts. And what was more wretched,
he missed out on heavenly life and did not enjoy this life either. At once, at the touch of warmth,

his flesh melted away, and the lover of life collapsed, having broken the law in vain. But when the guard saw that he had turned aside and run into the bathhouse, he placed himself in the position of the deserter.

[the guard] threw off his clothes and joined the naked men. He cried out the same call as the saints: "I am a Christian." By the suddenness of his change he worked a wonder for those watching. He filled up the number, and by adding himself he consoled them in the sorrow they felt over the one who had fled. In this he imitated the fighters in the front line,
who, when a man in the first rank of shields falls, at once fill up the troop, so that their front is not thrown into confusion by those who have fallen. In the same way
he too acted. He saw the heavenly wonders,
recognized the truth, ran to the Master, and was numbered with the martyrs.

He renewed what happened among the disciples: Judas departed, and Matthias came in to take his place. He became an imitator of Paul: yesterday a persecutor, today an evangelist. He too received his calling from above, not from men; nor did he come to faith through a man.
He was baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, into him, not by Paul but by his own faith,

not in water but in his own blood. And so, as day was beginning, they were handed over to the fire while still breathing, and what the fire left of them was scattered into the river, so that the passion of the blessed ones might pass through all creation. They struggled on the earth; they endured the cold.
They were handed over to fire; water received them.
Theirs is the voice: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment.” These are the ones who have embraced our land, like sons of an allotted portion.
They ward off invasions by enemies, not confining themselves to one place, but being present in many places and adorning many homelands. And it is glorious.
They were not divided one by one among those who receive them; rather, mingled together, they dance as one choir. O wonder!
They are not fewer in number, nor do they become more. Even if you divide them among a hundred, they do not go beyond their own
number; if you gather them into one, they are forty. And so they remain, after the nature of fire: for fire passes over to the one who kindles from it as well.
and he is wholly present with the one who possesses him. And the forty, too: all are together, and all are with each one.

A kindness without envy, grace that cannot be exhausted, ready help for Christians, an assembly of martyrs, victorious soldiers, a choir of those singing praise. How much would you labor to find, somehow,
even one person praying to the Lord for you! Here are forty sending up their prayer in harmony.
Where two or three are gathered in the Lord’s name, he is there among them. But where there are forty, who will still dispute that God’s presence is there?
Whoever is in sorrow, let him flee to the Forty; whoever rejoices, let him run to them: the one so that he may be delivered from his sorrow, and the other so that his joy may be preserved.
Here a faithful woman comes to pray for her children; she prays for the return of her husband who is away, and for the healing of one who is sick. Let your prayers be made together with the martyrs.
Let young men imitate those of their own age. Let fathers pray to be fathers of such children. And let mothers learn the story of the good mother.
The mother of one of the blessed ones, seeing them

The others had already died from the cold, but her own son was still breathing. Because of his strength and endurance of these cruel sufferings, the rulers left him behind, thinking that he might somehow change his mind. She herself took him in her own arms, lifted him onto her shoulder, and placed him on the wagon.
on which the others lay as they were being taken to the fire. Truly a martyr’s mother!
did not shed a weak tear, nor did she utter anything abject or unworthy of the occasion.

Instead she said: "Go, O son, on the good road with your companions of your own age and with your friends. Do not be separated from the company. Do not appear before the Master after the others, truly."
From a good root comes a good shoot as well. The noble mother showed that she had nourished him with the teachings of the good faith even more than with milk.
Having been brought up in this way, he was sent on his way like this by his faithful mother. And the devil went away in shame.
For, having stirred up all creation against them, he found it all overcome by the virtue of these men: the fiercely windy night, the frozen ground, the season, the nakedness of their bodies.
O holy company! O sacred assembly! O invincible host! O guardians of the whole human race, good companions in sorrow, helpers
in prayer, stars of the world, flowers of the Church!
The earth did not cover you, nor [?] did heaven receive you; the gates of paradise were opened.
It was a sight worthy of the angelic hosts, worthy of the patriarchs, the prophets, and the righteous: men in the very flower of youth who disregarded life,
who loved the Lord more than parents and more than children, while bearing the very bloom of life.
they despised this temporary life so that they might glorify God in their bodies.
Having become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings, they raised up those who had fallen.

They strengthened those who doubted and doubled the longing of the faithful. They all raised up one victory: the true faith. And they were adorned with one crown of righteousness, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
